title: Interest & APR
description: How interest builds, how APR differs from APY, and where fees hide.
wolfLine: The rate is the bite. The fee is the second bite.

apr.definition: Annual Percentage Rate: the yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percentage. Higher means more expensive.
apr.example: Borrow $1,000 at 10% APR for a year and it costs you about $100.

balance.definition: How much you still owe on a card or loan right now.
balance.example: Spend $700 on a card, pay back $200, and your balance is $500.

minimum-payment.definition: The smallest amount a lender lets you pay each month. Pay only this and your debt shrinks very slowly.
minimum-payment.example: You owe $2,000, but the card only asks for $40 this month.

simple-interest.definition: Interest worked out only on the principal: principal × rate × time.

origination-fee.definition: A fee some lenders charge for setting up a loan. It is part of the cost, on top of interest.
origination-fee.example: A $100 origination fee on a $2,000 loan adds $100 to what the loan costs you.

lessons.title: APR, Decoded
lessons.summary: What borrowing really costs you each year.

steps.context: Lenders show the yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage called the [[APR]]. A higher APR means more expensive debt.
steps.prompt: One card has a 12% APR. Another has 24%. Which is cheaper to borrow on?
steps.explain: Lower APR, lower cost.

steps.context: Rough yearly cost = amount you owe ├ù APR. Owe $1,000 at 10% APR for a year and it costs about $1,000 ├ù 0.10 = $100.
steps.prompt: You owe $2,000 on a card at 20% APR for a whole year. Roughly how much interest is that?
steps.explain: $2,000 ├ù 0.20 = $400. Cards add interest monthly, so the real number is a bit higher.

steps.context: The amount you still owe on a card or loan is your [[balance]].
steps.prompt: You spent $700 on your card and paid back $200. What’s your balance?
steps.explain: $700 ΓêÆ $200 = $500 still owed.

steps.context: Every month, a card asks for at least a small [[minimum payment]]. Pay only that, and interest keeps the balance alive for a very long time.
steps.prompt: What happens if you only ever pay the minimum?
choices: The debt is gone in a month
The card company forgives the rest
The debt drags on for years because of interest
steps.explain: Minimums are designed to keep you paying. Pay more whenever you can.

steps.context: Stretching a loan over more years makes each monthly payment smaller, but you pay interest for longer.
steps.prompt: A smaller monthly payment always means a cheaper loan.
steps.explain: Smaller payments over more years can cost more in total.

steps.prompt: APR stands for Annual Percentage ___.
steps.explain: Annual Percentage Rate.

lessons.title: Simple Interest
lessons.summary: Principal times rate times time. One clean formula.

steps.context: [[Simple interest]] is principal × rate × time. $1,000 at 8% for one year is $1,000 × 0.08 × 1 = $80. It does not add interest on the interest.
steps.prompt: What does simple interest get multiplied by?
choices: The principal, the rate, and the time
steps.explain: Principal × rate × time.

steps.prompt: $1,200 at 9% simple interest for 1 year. How much interest?
The same $1,200 at 9% for 3 years, simple interest. How much interest?
You borrow $800 at 5% simple interest for 2 years. How much do you pay back in total?
Simple interest charges interest on the interest from last year.
steps.explain: That would be compounding. Simple interest stays on the original principal.

steps.prompt: Simple interest equals principal × rate × ___.
steps.explain: How long you borrow is the third number.

lessons.title: Interest, Month by Month
lessons.summary: Cards usually charge interest every month, not once a year.

steps.context: A card’s [[APR]] is a yearly rate. Divide by 12 for a rough monthly rate. On a [[balance]] of $1,000 at 24% APR, one month of interest is about $1,000 × 0.02 = $20.
steps.prompt: A card lists 24% APR. About what monthly rate is that?
steps.explain: 24% ÷ 12 months = 2% a month.

steps.prompt: $1,000 balance, 24% APR. About how much interest in the first month?
You pay nothing. The balance becomes $1,020. About how much interest in the second month?
steps.explain: $1,020 × 0.02 = $20.40. The interest itself starts getting interest.

steps.prompt: $2,000 balance at 18% APR. Monthly rate is 1.5%. How much interest this month?
Paying the balance in full stops this month’s interest from piling onto next month.
steps.explain: Nothing left to charge. The [[minimum payment]] alone usually does not do that.

steps.prompt: Why is the second month’s interest higher if you pay nothing?
choices: The balance grew, so the rate hits a bigger number
The APR went up by itself
steps.explain: $20 of interest became part of the balance.

lessons.title: APR and APY
lessons.summary: One is the price of borrowing. The other is what savings earn.

steps.context: [[APR]] is the yearly cost of borrowing. [[APY]] is what savings earn in a year, counting interest on the interest. A 5% APR loan and a 5% APY savings account are not the same kind of deal.
steps.prompt: Which number is the yearly cost of borrowing?
steps.explain: APR is what a loan or card costs you.

steps.context: APY already includes compounding, so a one-year estimate is balance × APY.
steps.prompt: A savings account holds $2,000 at 4% APY for a year. About how much does it earn?
You owe $2,000 on a card at 20% APR for a year, and you pay nothing. Roughly how much interest?
steps.explain: $2,000 × 0.20 = $400. Monthly compounding makes the real bill a bit higher.

steps.prompt: You want a savings account to grow. Which number do you compare?
choices: The APR on someone else’s car loan
steps.explain: APY is the earnings number.

steps.prompt: A lower APR on a loan means cheaper borrowing.
steps.explain: Lower price to borrow.

steps.prompt: Why can a 20% APR card cost a bit more than balance × 0.20?
choices: Interest is added month by month, and then interest hits that too
Banks round every charge up to $100
steps.explain: The rough yearly figure is a floor, not the whole story.

lessons.title: Two Loan Offers
lessons.summary: The lower rate can still lose if a fee is riding along.

steps.context: Compare the total you pay back, not the rate alone.
steps.prompt: What is the interest on Loan A?
What do you pay back on Loan A, fee included?
What do you pay back on Loan B?
How much more does Loan B cost than Loan A?
Loan B’s interest rate is lower. Why does it still cost more?
choices: The $200 fee outweighs the cheaper interest
why: Both are real offers. One is just pricier.
steps.explain: $240 of interest plus a $200 fee is $440. Loan A’s interest is $320.

steps.prompt: The offer with the smaller interest line is always the cheaper loan.
steps.explain: Add the fee before you decide.

lessons.title: The Total Cost
lessons.summary: Monthly payments hide the real price. Multiply them.

steps.context: The total cost is every payment added up. Interest is that total minus the [[principal]].
steps.prompt: A $9,000 loan asks for $250 a month for 48 months. How much do you pay in total?
How much of that $12,000 is interest?
$150 a month for 36 months. What is the total?
That loan’s principal was $4,500. How much interest?
Two loans offer the same monthly payment. One lasts 3 years, one lasts 5. Which costs more in total?
steps.explain: Same payment, more months, more money.

steps.prompt: A smaller monthly payment can mean a higher total cost.
steps.explain: You are paying interest for longer.

lessons.title: Fees Inside the APR
lessons.summary: A fee is part of the price, even when the rate looks low.

steps.context: An [[origination fee]] is money the lender takes for setting up the loan. [[APR]] is meant to include fees like this, so you can compare offers. The interest rate alone can look cheaper than the loan really is.
steps.prompt: What is an origination fee?
choices: A charge for setting up the loan
steps.explain: It is part of the cost of borrowing.

steps.prompt: You borrow $2,000 for one year at 10% interest, plus a $100 origination fee. How much is the interest?
Add the fee. What did this loan cost you in the first year?
That $300 is what percent of the $2,000 you borrowed?
The interest rate and the APR can be different numbers when a loan has fees.
steps.explain: The APR rolls the fee into the yearly cost.

steps.prompt: Two loans both say 10% interest. One has a $100 fee and one has no fee. Which comparison do you trust?
choices: The APR, or the total dollars you pay
steps.explain: Dollars out the door beat a single percentage.

lessons.title: Maya’s Phone
lessons.summary: A small monthly number can double the price of a phone.

story.title: The phone plan
story.body:
Maya’s phone died. The shop will finance a **$840** phone: **$35** a month for **36** months. No money down.

She can also buy a refurbished phone for **$220** in cash. She has **$300** in savings and did not want to touch it.

steps.prompt: How much does Maya pay in total on the 36-month plan?
How much extra is that, above the $840 price?
How much does she save by paying $220 cash instead of the plan’s $1,260?
The $35 payment fits her month easily. What is still true?
choices: The plan costs $420 more than the phone’s price
steps.explain: A payment that fits can still be a bad price.

steps.prompt: Using $220 of her $300 savings leaves her with some cash still set aside.
What is the careful comparison?
choices: Total dollars, not the size of the monthly payment
steps.explain: 36 small payments hid a $420 charge.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Interest & APR
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: $2,500 at 8% simple interest for 2 years. How much interest?
$500 balance at 24% APR. About how much interest in one month? Use a 2% monthly rate.
A one-year loan charges $160 of interest and a $40 fee on $2,000 borrowed. What did the year cost?
APY is the yearly cost of a credit card.
steps.explain: APY is what savings earn. APR is the borrowing cost.
